newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spanish Treasury chief sees scope for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spanish Treasury chief sees scope for rate cut.

text.p: Long-term Spanish interest rates, at an all-time low, are giving the Bank of Spain room to cut official rates and save the country money on its interest payments, according to Treasury Director-General Jaime Caruana.

"The Treasury, following the market, has been reducing interest rates at every auction in a very speedy way. This gives the Bank of Spain scope," Caruana told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.

Yields on 10-year government bonds, or "bonos", have dropped dramatically in recent months as the new conservative government strove to instill fiscal discipline in Spain and ensure it would join the launch of the European single currency in 1999.
At the end of November, yields finally dropped beneath the historic barrier of seven percent amid growing market confidence in Spain's European pretensions.

Even more telling, the spread between Spanish and sturdier German bonds shrank to a minimum of 119 basis points on Tuesday from 330 in March and 500 in the summer of 1995, suggesting the risk of holding them had diminished sharply.
The Bank of Spain has sanctioned six cuts in its key money market rate this year, lowering it to the current 6.75 percent from nine percent in early January.

And the central bank, pleased by a decline in inflation and the new conservative government's tight fiscal policies, is widely expected to lower the interest rate yet one more time at its two remaining auctions this year.
But Caruana added that the decision is up to the central bank, which sets its policy to ensure stable prices.
"The Bank of Spain has to follow a monetary policy which procures stability in consumer prices," he said.
The decline in long-term rates is also relieving the burden on the Spanish purse, which has to pay less interest to service its outstanding public debt and should continue to help next year.

"We made the interest rate expenditure forecast (in the budget), which is 3.46 trillion pesetas, based on the yield curve at that time. Since then there has been significant reductions (in yields)," Caruana said.
He added that every full point fall in interest rates represents a savings of 400 billion pesetas, but the full effect is only felt after a few years.
"There are significant savings for the budget. The amount could be 130 billion pesetas if interest rates remain where they are now until the end of 1997," Caruana said.
